tutorial_example_entry.lesson_core_move: Identify the support and zero regions of a continuous-time signal from a graph, formula, or piecewise definition by marking the intervals where $x(t)$ is nonzero versus identically zero.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Signal Support and Zero Regions

image_slots.image_description: Clean continuous-time signal plot with a horizontal time axis labeled t and a vertical signal axis labeled $x(t)$. The signal is zero on the time axis for $t<1$, nonzero at a constant positive level on $1\let\le4$, and zero again for $t>4$. Highlight or bracket the interval [1,4] as the support, and label the left zero region $t<1 and the right zero region t>4$. Use simple integer tick marks, restrained highlighting, and no decorative elements.

blocks.text: A continuous-time signal is a function of time. At each time $t$, the signal value $x(t)$ is either zero or nonzero. Support and zero regions come from marking those two possibilities over intervals of time.
The support of a signal is the time region where the signal is nonzero. To identify support, scan along the time axis and mark the intervals where $x(t)\ne 0$.
A zero region is an interval where the signal is identically zero. This is stronger than saying the signal equals zero at one isolated time; every time in the interval must have value $0$.

blocks.latex: \text{zero region: an interval on which } x(t)=0 \text{ for every } t

blocks.text: In the picture, the signal is nonzero only on the middle interval. That interval is the support. The flat parts on the time axis before and after the support are zero regions because $x(t)=0$ for every time in those intervals.

The repeatable procedure is: first find where $x(t)\ne 0$ and write those intervals as the support. Then write the intervals where $x(t)=0$ throughout as the zero regions. The same procedure applies whether the signal is shown by a graph, a piecewise definition, or a formula.

image_slots.image_description: Clean continuous-time signal graph with horizontal axis labeled t and vertical axis labeled $x(t)$. The signal is zero on the time axis for $t<-2$, jumps to a constant positive value $x(t)=2 on -2\let\le3$, then returns to zero for $t>3$. Show readable integer tick marks at $t=-2 and t=3$, a simple piecewise signal trace, and clear nonzero support boundaries. Do not label the support interval or reveal the answer in the image.

example_content.example_prompt: The graph of $x(t)$ is shown. Identify the support of $x(t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue for support is where the graph is off the time axis. In this graph, the signal is zero before $t=-2$, then it becomes nonzero at $t=-2$.
The graph stays nonzero until $t=3$, and after $t=3$ it returns to the time axis. So the nonzero part starts at $-2$ and ends at $3$.
The support is only the interval where $x(t)\ne 0$. Times outside $[-2,3]$ are not part of the support because the graph lies on the time axis there.

example_content.example_prompt: The graph of $x(t)$ is shown. Identify the zero regions of $x(t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: First locate the nonzero part of the graph so it does not get included in a zero region. Here, the graph is above the time axis only between $t=-1$ and $t=2$.

A zero region is an interval where $x(t)=0$ for every time in that interval. The graph lies on the time axis for all times up to $-1$, and it lies on the time axis again for all times from $2$ onward.
The interval $(-1,2)$ is not a zero region because the graph is nonzero there. The zero regions are the outside intervals where the graph stays on $x(t)=0$ throughout.

sections.section_title: Finding Support and Zero Regions from a Piecewise Definition

example_content.example_prompt: For the piecewise signal with $x(t)=0$ for $t<-1$, $x(t)=2$ for $-1\le t<2$, $x(t)=0$ for $2\le t<4$, $x(t)=-1$ for $4\le t\le 5$, and $x(t)=0$ for $t>5$, identify the support and the zero regions.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that each row of the piecewise definition gives a signal value together with the time interval where that value applies. Rows with value $0$ contribute to zero regions, and rows with a nonzero value contribute to the support.
The nonzero rows are $x(t)=2$ on $-1\le t<2$ and $x(t)=-1$ on $4\le t\le 5$. Combining those intervals gives the support.
The zero-valued rows are $x(t)=0$ on $t<-1$, on $2\le t<4$, and on $t>5$. Combining those intervals gives the zero regions.

The endpoint symbols come directly from the original inequalities. For example, $-1$ belongs to the nonzero row, so it is included in the support, while $2$ belongs to the zero row, so it is included in a zero region.

sections.section_title: Finding Support and Zero Regions from a Formula

example_content.example_prompt: A signal is given by $x(t)=2e^{-t}$ for $0\le t\le 4$ and $x(t)=0$ otherwise. Identify the support and the zero regions of $x(t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that the formula is active only on the stated interval. Here, $x(t)=2e^{-t}$ applies for $0\le t\le 4$, and the signal is defined to be $0$ otherwise.
Next check whether the active formula is actually nonzero on that interval. Since $e^{-t}>0$ for every real $t$, the product $2e^{-t}$ is also positive for every $t$ from $0$ to $4$.
Because the signal is nonzero throughout the active interval, that interval is the support.
The phrase $x(t)=0$ otherwise means every time outside the active interval belongs to a zero region.

The endpoints $0$ and $4$ are included in the support because the formula applies at both endpoints and gives nonzero values there. The zero regions are open at those endpoints because $x(0)\ne 0$ and $x(4)\ne 0$.

sections.section_title: Distinguishing Isolated Zeros from Zero Regions

example_content.example_prompt: A signal is given by $x(t)=t$ for $-2\le t\le 2$ and $x(t)=0$ otherwise. Identify the zero regions, and decide whether $t=0$ is a zero region.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the same compact formula format as before: one formula is active on a stated interval, and the signal is zero otherwise. Here, $x(t)=t$ is active for $-2\le t\le 2$, so the otherwise-zero parts are outside that interval.
Now check whether the active formula itself ever equals zero. On the active interval, solving $x(t)=0$ means solving $t=0$.

The time $t=0$ is a single zero value inside the active interval. It is not a zero region because a zero region must be an interval where $x(t)=0$ for every time in the interval. Near $0$, values such as $x(0.5)=0.5$ and $x(-0.5)=-0.5$ are not zero.

explanation_blocks.latex: t=0\text{ is an isolated zero, not a zero region.}

explanation_blocks.text: So the zero regions are only the outside intervals where the signal is identically zero. Within the active interval, the nonzero portions are everything except the isolated zero at $t=0$.

prompt_blocks.text: The graph of $x(t)$ is shown. What is the support of $x(t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The support is the interval where the graph is nonzero. In the graph, $x(t)$ is off the time axis from $t=-3$ through $t=1$, and it is zero outside that interval.

prompt_blocks.text: The graph of $x(t)$ is shown. What is the support of $x(t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The graph is nonzero on two separate intervals: from $t=-4$ to $t=-2$, and from $t=1$ to $t=3$. The interval between them is not part of the support because the graph lies on the time axis there.

prompt_blocks.text: The graph of $x(t)$ is shown. Which intervals are zero regions of $x(t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A zero region is an interval where the graph lies on the time axis. The graph is on the time axis for all times up to $-3$, and again for all times from $1$ onward.

prompt_blocks.text: The graph of $x(t)$ is shown. Which intervals are zero regions of $x(t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The graph is on the time axis before $t=-2$, then it is nonzero from $-2$ up to but not including $3$. At $t=3$, the graph returns to the time axis and stays zero afterward.

sections.section_title: Finding Support and Zero Regions from a Piecewise Definition

prompt_blocks.text: For the piecewise definition below, which choice gives the support and zero regions of $x(t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The nonzero rows are $x(t)=3$ on $-2\le t<1$ and $x(t)=-2$ on $3\le t\le4$, so those intervals form the support. The rows where $x(t)=0$ form the zero regions.

prompt_blocks.text: For the piecewise definition below, which choice gives the support and zero regions of $x(t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The nonzero rows are $x(t)=-1$ on $-4<t\le-1$ and $x(t)=t+1$ on $2<t<5$. Since $t+1$ is nonzero throughout $2<t<5$, those two intervals form the support. The zero-valued rows give the zero regions, with endpoint inclusions copied from the inequalities.

sections.section_title: Finding Support and Zero Regions from a Formula

prompt_blocks.text: A signal is given by $x(t)=3e^{-t}$ for $0\le t\le 4$ and $x(t)=0$ otherwise. Which choice gives the support and zero regions of $x(t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The active formula applies on $0\le t\le4$. Since $3e^{-t}>0$ on that whole interval, the support is $[0,4]$. The word otherwise means the signal is zero outside that interval.

prompt_blocks.text: A signal is given by $x(t)=5e^{-t}$ for $-3<t\le 2$ and $x(t)=0$ otherwise. Which choice gives the support and zero regions of $x(t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The active interval is $-3<t\le2$, and $5e^{-t}$ is nonzero throughout that interval. The signal is zero otherwise, so the outside intervals become the zero regions. The endpoint $-3$ is excluded from the support and included in a zero region, while $2$ is included in the support.

sections.section_title: Distinguishing Isolated Zeros from Zero Regions

prompt_blocks.text: A signal is given by $x(t)=t-1$ for $-1\le t\le 3$ and $x(t)=0$ otherwise. Which statement correctly identifies the zero regions and explains the zero at $t=1$?

choice_blocks.text: The zero regions are $(-∞,-1)\cup(3,∞)$. The time $t=1$ is an isolated zero inside the active interval, not a zero region.
The zero regions are $(-∞,-1)\cup\{1\}\cup(3,∞)$, so $t=1$ is a zero region.
The zero regions are $(-∞,-1)\cup[1,∞)$, because $x(1)=0$ starts a zero region.
The entire active interval $[-1,3]$ should be removed from the support because it contains the zero value $x(1)=0$.
The zero region is $(-∞,∞)$, because every solution of $x(t)=0$ makes the signal zero everywhere.

questions.correct_answer: The zero regions are $(-∞,-1)\cup(3,∞)$, and $t=1$ is an isolated zero, not a zero region.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The signal is identically zero outside the active interval, so those outside intervals are zero regions. Inside the active interval, solving $t-1=0$ gives the single time $t=1$; nearby active values are not zero, so this is an isolated zero rather than a zero region.

answer_explanation_blocks.latex: \text{zero regions: }(-\infty,-1)\cup(3,\infty),\qquad t=1\text{ is an isolated zero.}

prompt_blocks.text: A signal is given by $x(t)=2t+4$ for $-3\le t\le 1$ and $x(t)=0$ otherwise. Which statement correctly identifies the zero regions and explains the zero at $t=-2$?

choice_blocks.text: The zero regions are $(-∞,-3)\cup(1,∞)$. The time $t=-2$ is an isolated zero inside the active interval, not a zero region.
The zero regions are $(-∞,-3)\cup\{-2\}\cup(1,∞)$, so $t=-2$ is a zero region.
The zero regions are $(-∞,-2]\cup[-2,∞)$, because the root $t=-2$ splits the time axis into zero regions.
The support is empty because the active formula equals zero at $t=-2$.
The zero regions are $(-∞,-3]\cup[1,∞)$, because the endpoints of the active interval must be included in the zero regions.

questions.correct_answer: The zero regions are $(-∞,-3)\cup(1,∞)$, and $t=-2$ is an isolated zero, not a zero region.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The signal is identically zero outside $[-3,1]$, so the outside intervals are zero regions. Solving $2t+4=0$ gives $t=-2$, but this is just one time inside the active interval; values near $-2$ are nonzero, so it is isolated rather than a zero region.

answer_explanation_blocks.latex: \text{zero regions: }(-\infty,-3)\cup(1,\infty),\qquad t=-2\text{ is an isolated zero.}
